title: Historical Background
desc: British constitutional developments in India before 1950

basic.q: Who was appointed as the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773?
basic.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the 'Governor-General of Bengal,' and Warren Hastings became the first to hold this office.

basic.q: In which year was the Supreme Court at Calcutta established?
basic.e: The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774 through a separate Act/Charter, following the Regulating Act of 1773.

basic.q: How many members did the Governor-General's Council consist of under the Regulating Act of 1773?
basic.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 provided for an Executive Council of four members to assist the Governor-General.

basic.q: Pitt's India Act of 1784 established a system of double government through the Court of Directors and which new body?
basic.e: Pitt's India Act, 1784 created a Board of Control to manage political affairs, while the Company's Court of Directors retained commercial affairs.

basic.q: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's trade monopoly in India except in the trade of which items?
basic.e: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's general trade monopoly but retained its monopoly over tea trade and trade with China.

basic.q: Who became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833?
basic.e: The Charter Act of 1833 converted the Governor-General of Bengal into the Governor-General of India, and Lord William Bentinck was the first to hold this position.

basic.q: Which new post was added to the Governor-General's Council by the Charter Act of 1833?
basic.e: The Charter Act of 1833 added a Law Member as a fourth member of the Governor-General's Council.

basic.q: The Charter Act of 1853 created a separate Legislative Council with how many additional 'legislative councillors'?
basic.e: The Charter Act of 1853 separated legislative and executive functions by adding six additional legislative councillors, forming a body that functioned like a mini-parliament.

basic.q: The Government of India Act of 1858 created which new office in Britain to oversee Indian affairs?
basic.e: Following the Revolt of 1857, the Government of India Act, 1858 abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors and created the office of Secretary of State for India.

basic.q: Who was the first Viceroy of India, a title created by the Government of India Act of 1858?
basic.e: The Government of India Act, 1858 gave the Governor-General the additional title of Viceroy, and Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.

basic.q: Which system, later becoming the basis of the modern cabinet system, was introduced by the Indian Councils Act of 1861?
basic.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 introduced the portfolio system, allowing Council members to be placed in charge of specific departments.

basic.q: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for which community for the first time?
basic.e: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims, earning Lord Minto the epithet 'Father of Communal Electorate.'

basic.q: Who became the first Indian to be appointed as a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council?
basic.e: Under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, Satyendra Prasad Sinha was appointed Law Member, becoming the first Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council.

basic.q: The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced 'dyarchy' at which level of government?
basic.e: The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced dyarchy in the provinces, dividing subjects into transferred and reserved categories.

basic.q: In which year was the Federal Court of India established under the Government of India Act of 1935?
basic.e: The Federal Court, a precursor to the Supreme Court, was established in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Regulating Act of 1773:
1. It made the Governor of Bengal the 'Governor-General of Bengal.'
2. It subordinated the Bombay and Madras Presidencies to Bengal in certain matters.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct: the Regulating Act of 1773 created the Governor-General of Bengal and subordinated Bombay and Madras to Bengal in certain matters.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about Pitt's India Act, 1784:
1. It established the Board of Control to manage political affairs.
2. It was the first Act to refer to Company territories in India as 'British possessions in India.'
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Pitt's India Act, 1784 created the Board of Control and was the first Act to term Company territories as 'British possessions in India.'

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1793:
1. It renewed the East India Company's charter for a period of 20 years.
2. It introduced significant constitutional changes in the structure of governance in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Charter Act of 1793 merely renewed the Company's charter for 20 years without introducing any major constitutional changes.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It ended the Company's trade monopoly in India completely, including the China trade.
2. It retained the Company's monopoly over trade in tea and with China.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Charter Act of 1813 ended most of the trade monopoly but retained the Company's monopoly over tea and China trade; complete abolition came only in 1833.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1833:
1. The Company ceased to be a commercial body and became a purely administrative body.
2. It successfully introduced open competition for recruitment to the civil service.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Charter Act of 1833 made the Company a purely administrative body, but its attempt at open competition for the civil service was unsuccessful.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1853:
1. It introduced open competition for the covenanted civil service based on the Macaulay Committee's recommendations.
2. It was the last of the Charter Acts and did not specify a fixed term for renewal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition (Macaulay Committee, 1854) and was the last Charter Act, with no fixed renewal term.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1858:
1. It abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.
2. It provided for a 15-member Council of India to assist the Secretary of State in an advisory capacity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Government of India Act, 1858 abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors and set up a 15-member Council of India to assist the Secretary of State.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1861:
1. It restored legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, beginning the process of decentralization.
2. Lord Canning nominated three Indians as non-official members of the legislative council.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Indian Councils Act, 1861 restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras and Lord Canning nominated three Indians as non-official members.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1892:
1. It increased the number of non-official members in the legislative councils and allowed them to discuss the budget.
2. It used the word 'election' explicitly to describe the method of choosing non-official members.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Indian Councils Act, 1892 expanded council functions and members, but the word 'election' was deliberately not used in the Act.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms):
1. It allowed Indians to become members of the Viceroy's Executive Council for the first time.
2. Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian member, holding the portfolio of Law Member.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 1909 Act allowed Indians onto the Viceroy's Executive Council for the first time, and Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first such member as Law Member.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1919:
1. It provided for a bicameral central legislature consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly.
2. It extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans in addition to Muslims.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Government of India Act, 1919 created a bicameral central legislature for the first time and extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1935:
1. It introduced provincial autonomy by abolishing dyarchy in the provinces.
2. It provided for the establishment of a Reserve Bank of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Government of India Act, 1935 introduced provincial autonomy (abolishing dyarchy in provinces) and provided for the Reserve Bank of India.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Independence Act, 1947:
1. It was based on the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.
2. It ended the paramountcy of the British Crown over the Indian princely states.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Indian Independence Act, 1947, based on the Mountbatten Plan, ended British Crown paramountcy over the princely states.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946:
1. It accepted the demand for a full separate sovereign state of Pakistan.
2. It proposed grouping British Indian provinces into Sections A, B, and C.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 rejected full Pakistan and instead proposed grouping provinces into Sections A, B, and C within a loose federal union.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the original composition of the Constituent Assembly of India:
1. It had a total of 389 members.
2. Of these, 93 members represented the Indian princely states.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Constituent Assembly originally had 389 members: 296 from British India's provinces and 93 from the princely states.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the Regulating Act of 1773 is NOT correct?
o: It made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal
It established the Supreme Court at Calcutta as part of the same Act, without any need for separate legislation
It subordinated the Bombay and Madras Presidencies to Bengal in certain matters
It provided for a four-member Executive Council for the Governor-General
advanced.e: The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774 via a separate Act/Charter, not directly by the Regulating Act of 1773 itself.

advanced.q: Which of the following was a specific contribution of Pitt's India Act, 1784, distinguishing it from the Regulating Act of 1773?
o: It established the Supreme Court at Calcutta
It created the Board of Control and for the first time termed Company territories as 'British possessions in India'
It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India
advanced.e: Pitt's India Act, 1784 uniquely created the Board of Control and first used the term 'British possessions in India'; the other options belong to different Acts.

advanced.q:
Arrange the following developments in the correct chronological sequence:
1. Ended the Company's trade monopoly except tea and China trade
2. Renewed the Company's charter for 20 years with no major changes
3. Ended the Company's trade monopoly completely
4. Was the last Charter Act, with no fixed renewal term
advanced.e: The correct order is Charter Act 1793 (renewal, no changes) → 1813 (partial monopoly end) → 1833 (complete monopoly end) → 1853 (last Charter Act).

advanced.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It ended the Company's trade monopoly in India for most goods.
2. It completely abolished all of the Company's trading privileges, including tea and China trade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
advanced.e: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the general trade monopoly, but tea and China trade privileges were abolished only later, by the Charter Act of 1833.

advanced.q: Why is the Charter Act of 1833's attempt at open competition for civil service recruitment considered 'unsuccessful'?
o: It was never legislated at all
Though provided for in the Act, it could not be effectively implemented, and open competition for the civil service was actually introduced later by the Charter Act of 1853
It applied only to the Madras Presidency
It was replaced immediately by a nomination system in the same year
advanced.e: The 1833 Act provided for open competition, but it was not effectively implemented; genuine open competition for the covenanted civil service came only with the 1853 Act.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Charter Act of 1853 from earlier Charter Acts?
o: It was the first Charter Act with no fixed term for renewal of the Company's charter
It first allowed Indians to become members of the legislative council
It first introduced dyarchy in the provinces
It ended the Company's trade monopoly in India
advanced.e: Unlike earlier Charter Acts renewed for fixed terms, the Charter Act of 1853 was the last one and specified no fixed renewal term.

advanced.q: The Government of India Act of 1858 is best understood in which of the following ways?
o: It transferred power from the Company to the Crown, without introducing any change to the legislative council's composition or functions
It transferred power from the Crown to the Company, while significantly expanding the legislative council
It introduced dyarchy while retaining Company rule in name
It abolished the post of Governor-General
advanced.e: The 1858 Act was primarily an administrative reorganization transferring power from Company to Crown; changes to the legislative council's composition came only with the Indian Councils Act of 1861.

advanced.q: Which of the following is a subtle but important distinction about the association of Indians with law-making under the Indian Councils Act of 1861?
o: Indians were elected members of the legislative council for the first time
Indians were nominated as non-official members, not elected, marking the first association of Indians with the law-making process
Indians were given a separate electorate for the first time
Indians formed a majority in the legislative council
advanced.e: Under the 1861 Act, Lord Canning nominated Indians as non-official members; this was association, not election, which came only later.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about elections to legislative councils under the Indian Councils Act of 1892 is most accurate?
o: It introduced full direct elections based on adult franchise
It introduced a limited, indirect form of elections, though the word 'election' was deliberately not used in the Act
It introduced separate electorates for Muslims
It introduced elections only for Sikhs and Anglo-Indians
advanced.e: The 1892 Act allowed non-official members to be recommended by certain bodies, an indirect election-like mechanism, without ever using the word 'election.'

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly captures a feature of the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 that is often confused with later reforms?
o: It introduced separate electorates for Muslims and, in the same Act, for Sikhs and Anglo-Indians as well
It introduced separate electorates only for Muslims; separate electorates for Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans were introduced later by the Government of India Act, 1919
It gave Indians a majority in the Viceroy's Executive Council
It introduced dyarchy in the provinces
advanced.e: The 1909 Act introduced separate electorates only for Muslims; extension to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans occurred only under the 1919 Act.

advanced.q: Which of the following is an accurate but easily overlooked distinction of the Government of India Act, 1919?
o: It introduced dyarchy at the centre while retaining unitary government in the provinces
It introduced dyarchy in the provinces (dividing subjects into transferred and reserved), while the centre continued without dyarchy
It abolished the office of Viceroy
It merged the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly into a single unicameral house
advanced.e: Dyarchy under the 1919 Act applied only to the provinces; dyarchy at the centre was proposed only later, by the 1935 Act, and even then never implemented.

advanced.q:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1935:
1. Dyarchy was abolished in the provinces and provincial autonomy was introduced.
2. Dyarchy was introduced at the centre, though it was never actually implemented.
3. The proposed All-India Federation came into effect in 1937 along with the Federal Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
advanced.e: The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and proposed (but never implemented) dyarchy at the centre; the All-India Federation never came into being, though the Federal Court was set up in 1937.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Indian Independence Act, 1947 from the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 regarding the question of Pakistan?
o: Both rejected the creation of Pakistan

The Cabinet Mission Plan rejected a full separate Pakistan and proposed grouping of provinces instead, whereas the Indian Independence Act, 1947 actually created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 proposed grouping of provinces into Sections A, B and C
The Cabinet Mission Plan created the dominion of Pakistan
advanced.e: The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) rejected full Pakistan, but the Indian Independence Act (1947), based on the Mountbatten Plan, actually created the two dominions of India and Pakistan.

advanced.q: A common misconception about the framing of India's Constitution is corrected by which fact regarding the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946?
o: Constituent Assembly members were directly elected by the people through universal adult franchise
Constituent Assembly members were indirectly elected by the provincial legislative assemblies, at roughly one member per million population
Constituent Assembly members were all nominated by the Viceroy
Constituent Assembly members were selected only from princely states
advanced.e: The Cabinet Mission Plan proposed indirect election of Constituent Assembly members by provincial legislative assemblies, not universal adult franchise, a fact often misunderstood.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly explains the change in the Constituent Assembly's total membership after August 1947?
o: It increased from 389 to over 400 due to new nominations
It decreased from 389 to about 299, mainly due to the Muslim League's withdrawal following Partition
It remained unchanged at 389 despite Partition
It decreased to 296 as all princely state representatives withdrew
advanced.e: Following Partition and the Muslim League's withdrawal, the Constituent Assembly's membership fell from 389 to about 299.

title: Making of the Constitution
desc: Constituent Assembly formation, drafting process and key dates

basic.q: In which year did the Cabinet Mission Plan, under which the Constituent Assembly was formed, come to India?
basic.e: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 provided the framework for the formation of the Constituent Assembly, whose members were indirectly elected by the provincial legislative assemblies.

basic.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly hold its first meeting?
basic.e: The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on 9 December 1946.

basic.q: Who was elected as the temporary/provisional Chairman of the Constituent Assembly at its first sitting, being the oldest member present?
basic.e: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, as the oldest member present, was elected the temporary chairman on 9 December 1946.

basic.q: Who was elected the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946?
basic.e: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.

basic.q: Who served as the Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly?
basic.e: H.C. Mukherjee served as the Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly under President Rajendra Prasad.

basic.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly?
basic.e: The Objectives Resolution was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946.

basic.q: On what date was the Objectives Resolution adopted by the Constituent Assembly?
basic.e: The Objectives Resolution was moved on 13 December 1946 but adopted only on 22 January 1947.

basic.q: When was the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly constituted?
basic.e: The Drafting Committee was constituted on 29 August 1947 with seven members.

basic.q: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee?
basic.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, earning him the title 'Father of the Constitution'.

basic.q: Who served as the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly and prepared the original draft constitution?
basic.e: Sir B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Advisor, prepared the initial draft which was then examined by the Drafting Committee.

basic.q: What was the original total strength of the Constituent Assembly as envisaged under the Cabinet Mission Plan?
basic.e: The original strength was 389 members: 296 from British Indian provinces and 93 from princely states.

basic.q: After the withdrawal of the Muslim League members following Partition, what was the reduced strength of the Constituent Assembly?
basic.e: Following Partition and the Muslim League's withdrawal, the Assembly's strength was reduced to 299.

basic.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly formally adopt the Constitution of India?
basic.e: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949, now celebrated as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Diwas).

basic.q: On which date did most provisions of the Constitution of India come into force?
basic.e: Most provisions commenced on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.

basic.q: Approximately how long did the Constituent Assembly take to complete the drafting of the Constitution?
basic.e: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to complete drafting the Constitution.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Objectives Resolution:
1. It was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946.
2. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946 and it was adopted on 22 January 1947.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Drafting Committee constituted on 29 August 1947:
1. It originally had seven members.
2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was its Chairman.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Drafting Committee had seven original members with Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as Chairman.

intermediate.q:
With reference to the committees of the Constituent Assembly, consider the following pairs:
1. Union Powers Committee : Jawaharlal Nehru
2. Provincial Constitution Committee : Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
3. Steering Committee : Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
intermediate.e: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct. The Steering Committee was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, not Ambedkar.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Muslim League and the Constituent Assembly:
1. The Muslim League boycotted the first session of the Constituent Assembly held on 9 December 1946.
2. The Muslim League members withdrew from the Assembly altogether after Partition was decided.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Muslim League boycotted the first session and later withdrew entirely once Partition was decided, reducing the Assembly's strength.

intermediate.q:
With reference to the original seven members of the Drafting Committee, consider the following statements:
1. N. Madhava Rau was a member from the very beginning of the Committee.
2. T.T. Krishnamachari joined the Committee as a replacement after the death of D.P. Khaitan.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: N. Madhava Rau replaced B.L. Mitter (who resigned due to health) and was not an original member, whereas T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan after his death in 1948.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the composition of the Constituent Assembly:
1. Members were elected directly by the people of India through universal adult franchise.
2. Members were indirectly elected by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies.
Which of the statements given above is correct?
intermediate.e: Members of the Constituent Assembly were indirectly elected by the provincial legislative assemblies, not by direct universal franchise.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
2. Sir B.N. Rau prepared the original draft of the Constitution before the Drafting Committee took it up.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; B.N. Rau prepared the initial draft, which the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar then examined and revised.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the original composition of the Constituent Assembly under the Cabinet Mission Plan:
1. 296 seats were allotted to British Indian provinces.
2. 93 seats were allotted to the princely states.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct, together making up the original strength of 389 members (296 + 93).

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the finalization of the Constitution:
1. The Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949.
2. Members of the Constituent Assembly signed the final copy of the Constitution on 24 January 1950.
3. The Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
intermediate.e: All three statements are correct: adoption (26 Nov 1949), signing (24 Jan 1950), and commencement (26 Jan 1950) were distinct events.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following pairs of committees of the Constituent Assembly with their chairmen:
1. Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal & Excluded Areas — Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
2. States Committee — Jawaharlal Nehru
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
intermediate.e: Both pairs are correctly matched; the Advisory Committee was chaired by Patel and the States Committee by Nehru.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Dr. Rajendra Prasad:
1. He was elected the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.
2. He was also the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct, but the Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, not Rajendra Prasad.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Objectives Resolution:
1. It laid down the fundamentals and philosophy of the constitutional structure.
2. It later formed the basis of the Preamble to the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; the Objectives Resolution shaped the Constitution's philosophy and became the basis of the Preamble.

intermediate.q:
With reference to the naming of days associated with the Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. 26 November is celebrated as 'Constitution Day' or 'Samvidhan Diwas'.
2. This observance has been officially followed since 2015.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; 26 November has been observed as Constitution Day since 2015.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Union Constitution Committee and the Union Powers Committee:
1. Both committees were chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
2. Both committees dealt with entirely unrelated subjects having no connection with each other.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct; both committees were chaired by Nehru, but they were closely related, both dealing with the structure and powers of the Union, so statement 2 is incorrect.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about sources of the Indian Constitution:
1. The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
2. The concept of the Concurrent List was borrowed from the Australian Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both are correct; DPSP came from the Irish Constitution and the Concurrent List from the Australian Constitution.

advanced.q: The date 26 January was chosen for the commencement of the Constitution primarily to commemorate which earlier event?
o: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly
The adoption of the Objectives Resolution
The declaration of 'Purna Swaraj' by the Indian National Congress in 1930
The formation of the Drafting Committee
advanced.e: 26 January was deliberately chosen because the Indian National Congress had declared 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence) on 26 January 1930.

advanced.q: Which member of the original Drafting Committee resigned due to ill health and was replaced by N. Madhava Rau?
advanced.e: B.L. Mitter resigned due to health reasons and was replaced by N. Madhava Rau, distinct from D.P. Khaitan who died and was replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari.

advanced.q: Which single source is regarded as having contributed the largest number of provisions to the Indian Constitution, including the federal scheme, office of Governor, and emergency provisions?
advanced.e: The Government of India Act, 1935 is the single largest source, contributing the federal scheme, office of governor, judiciary, public service commissions and emergency provisions.

advanced.q: Which of the following borrowed features is correctly matched with its source constitution?
o: 'Procedure established by law' — Constitution of Japan
advanced.e: 'Procedure established by law' was borrowed from the Constitution of Japan. Judicial review comes from the US, DPSP from Ireland, and the Concurrent List from Australia — making the other pairs incorrect.

advanced.q: The provision for suspension of Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency in the Indian Constitution draws inspiration from which constitution?
advanced.e: The emergency provisions, including suspension of Fundamental Rights, were influenced by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

advanced.q: The method of election of the President of India was influenced by the constitution of which country?
advanced.e: The Irish Constitution influenced the method of election of the President of India, along with the DPSP and Rajya Sabha nominations.

advanced.q: The procedure for amendment of the Indian Constitution is said to have been borrowed from the constitution of which country?
advanced.e: India's constitutional amendment procedure is traceable to the South African Constitution.

advanced.q: The concept of 'advisory jurisdiction' of the Supreme Court of India is traceable to the constitutional practice of which country?
advanced.e: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court was borrowed from the Canadian Constitution.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the role of Sir B.N. Rau from that of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the constitution-making process?
o: Rau chaired the Drafting Committee while Ambedkar was Constitutional Advisor
Rau was the Constitutional Advisor who prepared the initial draft, while Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee that examined and revised it
Rau chaired the Steering Committee while Ambedkar was Vice-President
advanced.e: B.N. Rau, as Constitutional Advisor, prepared the preliminary draft; the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar's chairmanship then scrutinised and revised it clause by clause.

advanced.q: With reference to the Constituent Assembly, which of the following correctly explains the difference between Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha and Dr. Rajendra Prasad?
o: Sinha was the permanent President while Prasad was the provisional Chairman
Sinha was elected provisional/temporary Chairman on 9 December 1946 as the oldest member present, while Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946
Both were elected on the same day to the same post
Sinha chaired the Drafting Committee while Prasad chaired the Union Powers Committee
advanced.e: Sinha was only the temporary chairman for the first sitting, while Rajendra Prasad was subsequently elected the permanent President two days later.

advanced.q: Consider the numerical composition of the Constituent Assembly. Which of the following best explains the change in its strength from 389 to 299?
o: It was due to the merger of certain princely states before the Assembly's first sitting
It was due to withdrawal of Muslim League members and adjustments following Partition
It was due to resignation of nominated members over the Objectives Resolution
It was due to expansion after accession of Jammu and Kashmir
advanced.e: The reduction from 389 to 299 occurred mainly because Muslim League members withdrew and adjustments followed the Partition of India.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the Objectives Resolution is NOT correct?
o: It was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946
It was moved as a proposal to establish India as an absolute monarchy
It later formed the basis of the Preamble
advanced.e: The Objectives Resolution envisaged India as a sovereign, democratic republic guaranteeing justice, liberty and equality — it never proposed an absolute monarchy, making this statement incorrect.

advanced.q: Regarding the 'Union Powers Committee' and the 'Union Constitution Committee' of the Constituent Assembly, which statement is most accurate?
o: Both were separate committees but both were chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru
They were the same committee under two different names with no chairman
Union Powers Committee was chaired by Patel and Union Constitution Committee by Nehru
Only one of these committees actually existed
advanced.e: Both the Union Powers Committee and the Union Constitution Committee were distinct committees, each chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.

advanced.q: Which of the following members did NOT originally serve on the seven-member Drafting Committee at the time of its constitution on 29 August 1947, despite later becoming closely associated with the drafting process?
advanced.e: T.T. Krishnamachari joined the Drafting Committee later, replacing D.P. Khaitan after his death in 1948, and was not among the original seven members.

advanced.q: The nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha and the procedure for election of Rajya Sabha members are said to be inspired respectively by which constitutions?
o: Irish Constitution and South African Constitution
advanced.e: Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from the Irish Constitution, while the election procedure for its members was borrowed from the South African Constitution.

title: Salient Features of the Constitution
desc: Core defining features of India's Constitution

basic.q: Which of the following best describes the Indian Constitution when compared with other constitutions of the world?
o: It is the shortest written constitution among sovereign countries
It is the lengthiest and most detailed written constitution of any sovereign country
It is an unwritten constitution like that of the UK
It is a purely rigid constitution with no scope for amendment
basic.e: The Indian Constitution is widely regarded as the lengthiest and most detailed written constitution of any sovereign country in the world.

basic.q: As originally adopted on 26 November 1949, how many Articles did the Constitution of India contain?
basic.e: The original Constitution (1949) contained 395 Articles, though this has grown due to subsequent amendments.

basic.q: The original Constitution of India, as adopted in 1949, was divided into how many Parts?
basic.e: The Constitution as originally adopted had 22 Parts; it now has about 25 Parts due to amendments.

basic.q: How many Schedules did the original Constitution of India (1949) contain?
basic.e: The original Constitution had 8 Schedules; the number has since increased to about 12 through amendments.

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution lays down the procedure for its amendment?
basic.e: Article 368 contains the procedure for amendment of the Constitution, reflecting its blend of rigidity and flexibility.

basic.q: The parliamentary form of government at the Union level is provided for under which Articles of the Constitution?
basic.e: Articles 74 and 75 establish the parliamentary executive at the Union level, with a Council of Ministers headed by the PM aiding the President.

basic.q: Which Articles establish the parliamentary system of government at the State level?
basic.e: Articles 163 and 164 provide for a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor.

basic.q: Scholars like K.C. Wheare describe the Indian federal system, marked by a strong centre, as:
o: Unitary only, with no federal features
basic.e: K.C. Wheare called India's system 'quasi-federal', since it combines federal features with a strong unitary bias.

basic.q: India has a single, integrated judicial system with which court at its apex?
basic.e: Unlike the dual court system of the USA, India has one integrated judiciary topped by the Supreme Court, enforcing both Union and State laws.

basic.q: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?
basic.e: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35) are contained in Part III, inspired mainly by the US Bill of Rights.

basic.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
basic.e: The DPSP (Articles 36 to 51) are in Part IV, borrowed from the Irish Constitution.

basic.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
basic.e: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

basic.q: Which model of citizenship does the Indian Constitution provide for?
o: Dual citizenship of state and nation
Single, uniform citizenship for the whole country
basic.e: Despite being a federal polity, India follows single/uniform citizenship, unlike the USA's dual citizenship model.

basic.q: Universal Adult Franchise in India is provided for under which Article?
basic.e: Article 326 provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies to be on the basis of universal adult franchise.

basic.q: The emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution were largely inspired by the constitution of which country?
basic.e: The emergency provisions (Articles 352-360) were inspired by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about amendment of the Constitution under Article 368:
1. Provisions not specifically covered under Article 368, such as certain matters relating to creation of new states, can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament.
2. Provisions like the election of the President require special majority of Parliament plus ratification by at least half the state legislatures.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct and illustrate the three methods of amendment under Article 368, showing the blend of rigidity and flexibility.

intermediate.q:
Which of the following require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures, in addition to a special majority of Parliament, for their amendment?
1. Election of the President
2. Representation of States in Parliament
3. Article 368 itself
4. Creation of a new State
intermediate.e: Federal provisions such as the election of the President, representation of states, and Article 368 itself need state ratification; creation of new states needs only a simple majority.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is correctly matched with respect to the federal-unitary blend of the Indian Constitution?
o: Dual polity of Union and States - unitary feature
Independent judiciary as adjudicator of disputes - unitary feature
Emergency provisions enabling a unitary character - unitary bias
Division of powers via Union, State and Concurrent Lists - unitary feature
intermediate.e: Emergency provisions allow the normally federal structure to function in a unitary manner, representing the Constitution's unitary bias.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy:
1. They are borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
2. Though non-justiciable, Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The DPSP were indeed borrowed from Ireland and, per Article 37, are fundamental to governance despite being non-justiciable.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about Fundamental Duties:
1. Ten Fundamental Duties were originally added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
2. An eleventh duty, on parents/guardians providing education opportunities to children aged 6-14, was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Originally 10 duties were added in 1976; the 11th duty on children's education was added later by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

intermediate.q: The voting age for elections in India was reduced from 21 years to 18 years by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
intermediate.e: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age under Article 326 from 21 to 18 years.

intermediate.q:
Which of the following are independent constitutional bodies established by the Constitution to safeguard Indian democracy?
1. Election Commission of India
2. Comptroller and Auditor General
3. Union and State Public Service Commissions
4. NITI Aayog
intermediate.e: The Election Commission, CAG, and Public Service Commissions are constitutional bodies; NITI Aayog is a non-constitutional executive body, not created by the Constitution.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the three types of emergencies under Part XVIII of the Constitution:
1. National Emergency, President's Rule, and Financial Emergency are all provided for.
2. During such emergencies, the normal federal structure can function in a unitary manner.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Part XVIII (Articles 352-360) provides for all three types of emergency, during which the polity can operate in a unitary fashion.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, 1992:
1. They added Panchayats as rural local government under Part IX.
2. They added Municipalities as urban local government under Part IXA.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 73rd Amendment added Panchayats (Part IX) and the 74th Amendment added Municipalities (Part IXA), creating a third tier of government.

intermediate.q: The Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution are mainly inspired by the Bill of Rights of which country?
intermediate.e: Part III of the Constitution, containing the Fundamental Rights, draws its main inspiration from the US Bill of Rights.

intermediate.q: According to the Preamble, India is described as a:
intermediate.e: The Preamble describes India as a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the current size of the Indian Constitution:
1. It now has approximately 470 Articles.
2. It now has approximately 25 Parts.
3. It now has approximately 12 Schedules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Due to amendments over time, the Constitution now has approximately 470 Articles, 25 Parts, and 12 Schedules — approximate because articles have been added and repealed.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements distinguishing Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles:
1. Fundamental Rights are justiciable, while Directive Principles are non-justiciable.
2. Fundamental Rights can be enforced through courts under Article 32, while Directive Principles cannot be enforced but are fundamental in governance.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Fundamental Rights are enforceable via Article 32, whereas DPSPs are non-justiciable yet fundamental to governance under Article 37.

intermediate.q: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution on the recommendation of which committee?
intermediate.e: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the inclusion of Fundamental Duties, later added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements best captures the paradox of India's federal polity with respect to citizenship?
o: India follows dual citizenship despite having a unitary government
India follows single citizenship despite being a federal polity with Union and States
India follows no citizenship system despite being federal
India follows state-based citizenship due to its unitary bias
intermediate.e: Even though India has a federal, dual polity of Union and States, it follows only single/uniform citizenship, unlike the USA.

advanced.q: Under Article 368, which method of amendment applies to provisions of the Constitution not specifically listed in the proviso to Article 368, such as certain citizenship-related matters?
o: Simple majority of Parliament, as in ordinary legislation
Special majority of Parliament plus ratification by half the states
Such provisions cannot be amended at all
advanced.e: Provisions outside the proviso to Article 368 (e.g., some citizenship matters, creation of new states) can be amended by a simple majority, like ordinary law-making.

advanced.q: Which of the following precisely describes 'special majority' as required under Article 368 for most constitutional amendments?
o: A simple majority of members present and voting
A majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting
Three-fourths of the total membership of each House
A majority of total membership of each House only
advanced.e: Special majority under Article 368 requires a majority of the total membership of each House AND a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

advanced.q: The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) is significant in the context of Article 368 because it:
o: Held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights at all
Established the 'basic structure' doctrine, limiting Parliament's amending power
Abolished the requirement of state ratification for federal provisions
advanced.e: The Kesavananda Bharati case established the 'basic structure' doctrine, holding that Parliament's amending power under Article 368, though wide, cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure.

advanced.q: Unlike the United States, where separate federal and state court systems exist, the Indian judicial system is best described as:
o: A dual court system similar to the USA
An independent and integrated judiciary, with a single system of courts enforcing both Union and State laws
A judiciary with no power of judicial review
A judiciary entirely subordinate to the Union Executive
advanced.e: India has an independent and integrated judiciary topped by the Supreme Court, with one hierarchy of courts enforcing both Union and State laws, unlike the USA's dual system.

advanced.q: Article 32, described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution, primarily enables:
o: Enforcement of Directive Principles of State Policy
Enforcement of Fundamental Rights through constitutional remedies
Amendment of the Constitution by simple majority
Imposition of President's Rule in states
advanced.e: Article 32 guarantees the right to constitutional remedies, making the Fundamental Rights justiciable and enforceable directly by the Supreme Court.

advanced.q: Although Directive Principles of State Policy are non-justiciable, which Article declares them to be fundamental in the governance of the country?
advanced.e: Article 37 states that the DPSP, while not enforceable by any court, are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly pairs a Part of the Constitution with the foreign source that primarily inspired it?
o: Part III (Fundamental Rights) - USA; Part IV (DPSP) - Ireland; Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) - erstwhile USSR
Part III (Fundamental Rights) - Ireland; Part IV (DPSP) - USA; Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) - UK
Part III (Fundamental Rights) - USSR; Part IV (DPSP) - USA; Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) - Ireland
Part III (Fundamental Rights) - UK; Part IV (DPSP) - USSR; Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) - Ireland
advanced.e: Fundamental Rights were inspired by the US Bill of Rights, DPSP by the Irish Constitution, and Fundamental Duties by the erstwhile USSR Constitution.

advanced.q: The eleventh Fundamental Duty, added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, obligates whom to do what?
o: The State to provide free legal aid to all citizens
Parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14 years
Every citizen to vote compulsorily in elections
Every citizen to pay income tax honestly
advanced.e: The 11th Fundamental Duty requires parents or guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6 to 14 years, complementing Article 21A.

advanced.q: Which of the following is an accurate characterization of the tension in India's federal design?
o: India has dual citizenship along with a unitary government
India has single citizenship despite having a dual polity of Union and States, a feature associated with its unitary bias
India has multiple citizenships corresponding to each state, reflecting strong federalism
India abolished federalism entirely in favour of a unitary state
advanced.e: Despite a dual polity (Union and States) and division of powers, India's single citizenship is one of several features giving the Constitution a unitary tilt.

advanced.q: During the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352, which of the following best describes the effect on the federal structure?
o: States gain complete legislative independence from the Centre
The normally federal structure can function in a unitary manner, with the Centre empowered over State subjects
Fundamental Rights are enhanced and cannot be restricted
advanced.e: During a National Emergency, the federal structure functions in a unitary manner, with Parliament empowered to legislate even on State List subjects.

advanced.q: K.C. Wheare's description of India as 'quasi-federal' and the popular characterization 'federal in form, unitary in spirit' both refer to which feature of the Constitution?
o: The purely unitary nature of Indian government with no federal features
The blend of federal structure with a strong unitary bias built into the Constitution
The absence of any division of powers between Centre and States
The complete independence of States from the Union in all matters
advanced.e: Both phrases capture how India combines a federal structure (dual polity, division of powers) with features like a strong centre and emergency powers that give it a unitary bias.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly matches the constitutional amendment, the tier of local government it introduced, and the Part of the Constitution under which it falls?
o: 73rd Amendment - Municipalities - Part IX; 74th Amendment - Panchayats - Part IXA
73rd Amendment - Panchayats - Part IX; 74th Amendment - Municipalities - Part IXA
73rd Amendment - Panchayats - Part IVA; 74th Amendment - Municipalities - Part V
73rd Amendment - Municipalities - Part IVA; 74th Amendment - Panchayats - Part IX
advanced.e: The 73rd Amendment introduced Panchayats under Part IX, and the 74th Amendment introduced Municipalities under Part IXA, forming the third tier of government.

advanced.q: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted into the Preamble of the Constitution by which amendment, the same amendment that also added Fundamental Duties?
advanced.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble and simultaneously added the Fundamental Duties in Part IVA.

advanced.q: A key criticism of the emergency provisions, borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany, is that they:
o: Make the judiciary the sole custodian of emergency powers
Enable the conversion of the normally federal structure into a unitary one, concentrating power at the Centre
Abolish Fundamental Rights permanently once invoked
Have never been invoked in India's constitutional history
advanced.e: Critics note that emergency provisions, inspired by the Weimar Constitution, allow the Centre to override the federal balance and function in a unitary manner, which can be misused.

advanced.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the parliamentary system adopted by India from a presidential system?
o: A directly elected President who is also the real executive head
A nominal head of state and a real executive (Council of Ministers headed by the PM/CM) collectively responsible to the legislature
Complete separation of powers between executive and legislature with no overlap
Fixed tenure of the executive independent of legislative confidence
advanced.e: India's parliamentary system, modeled on the Westminster system, features a nominal head of state (President/Governor) and a real executive collectively responsible to the legislature.

title: Preamble
desc: Preamble text, amendments, and key court rulings

basic.q: The Preamble to the Indian Constitution begins with which words?
basic.e: The Preamble begins with the words WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, indicating that the Constitution derives its authority from the people.

basic.q: As per the Preamble, India is described as a:
basic.e: The Preamble describes India as a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC after the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

basic.q: According to the Preamble, the Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
basic.e: The Preamble states this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949 as the date of adoption of the Constitution, distinct from its commencement on 26 January 1950.

basic.q: Which date is mentioned in the Preamble for adoption of the Constitution, and what is it not to be confused with?
o: 26 January 1950; not to be confused with 26 November 1949 (commencement)
15 August 1947; not to be confused with 26 January 1950
26 November 1949; not to be confused with 26 January 1950 (commencement)
9 December 1946; not to be confused with 26 November 1949
basic.e: The date twenty-sixth day of November, 1949 in the Preamble is the date of adoption by the Constituent Assembly, while the Constitution actually commenced on 26 January 1950.

basic.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act inserted the words Socialist and Secular into the Preamble?
basic.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, enacted during the Emergency, inserted Socialist, Secular and Integrity into the Preamble.

basic.q: As originally adopted in 1949, the Preamble described India as a:
basic.e: The original 1949 Preamble described India merely as a SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC, without the words Socialist and Secular.

basic.q: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 was based on the recommendations of which committee?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 was enacted based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

basic.q: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 was enacted during the government headed by:
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 was enacted during the Emergency, under the government headed by Indira Gandhi.

basic.q: Which word did the 42nd Amendment Act insert to change the phrase unity of the Nation to unity and integrity of the Nation in the Preamble?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment added the word Integrity, changing the phrase to unity and integrity of the Nation.

basic.q: How many times has the Preamble to the Indian Constitution been amended so far?
basic.e: The Preamble has been amended only once so far, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

basic.q: As per the Preamble, JUSTICE is to be secured to all citizens in which spheres?
basic.e: The Preamble secures JUSTICE - social, economic and political - to all citizens.

basic.q: As per the Preamble, LIBERTY is assured of:
o: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
basic.e: The Preamble assures LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.

basic.q: As per the Preamble, EQUALITY is assured of:
basic.e: The Preamble assures EQUALITY of status and of opportunity.

basic.q: As per the Preamble, FRATERNITY is meant to assure:
o: The dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation
basic.e: FRATERNITY promotes among citizens the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.

basic.q: The Preamble ends with the Constituent Assembly declaring that it does hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves:
basic.e: The Preamble concludes with the Constituent Assembly declaring that it does hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the words added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: 1. The word Socialist was added. 2. The word Secular was added. 3. The word Republic was added. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 42nd Amendment added Socialist and Secular (along with Integrity); the word Republic was already present in the original 1949 Preamble.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the Preamble: 1. The original 1949 Preamble described India as a Sovereign Democratic Republic. 2. The word Integrity was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct: the 1949 Preamble read Sovereign Democratic Republic, and Integrity was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Berubari Union case (1960) held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. 2. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: In Berubari Union (1960), the Supreme Court held the Preamble was not part of the Constitution; in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), it overruled this view and held the Preamble is part of the Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the date mentioned in the Preamble: 1. This twenty-sixth day of November, 1949 refers to the date the Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly. 2. The Constitution commenced (came into force) on the same date, 26 November 1949. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Preamble's date refers to adoption (26 November 1949); the Constitution actually commenced on 26 January 1950, a different date.

intermediate.q: Consider the following pairs of ideals in the Preamble and their content: 1. Justice - social, economic and political. 2. Liberty - of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. 3. Equality - of status, opportunity and wealth. Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
intermediate.e: Justice and Liberty are correctly matched as per the Preamble; Equality is assured of status and of opportunity only, not wealth.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the LIC of India case (1995): 1. The Supreme Court held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution. 2. The case reversed the position taken in the Kesavananda Bharati case. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: In the LIC of India case (1995), the Supreme Court reiterated (not reversed) that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution, consistent with Kesavananda Bharati.

intermediate.q: With reference to the Preamble, consider the following statements: 1. The Preamble is enforceable in a court of law like the Fundamental Rights. 2. The source of the Constitution's authority, as per the Preamble, lies with the people of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Preamble is not directly enforceable in court unlike Fundamental Rights, but it does affirm that the Constitution's authority derives from the people of India.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding amendments to the Preamble: 1. The Preamble has been amended only once so far. 2. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 was the amendment that changed the Preamble. 3. The words added were Socialist, Secular and Integrity. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three statements are correct regarding the sole amendment to the Preamble made by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Kesavananda Bharati case held that the Preamble can never be amended under Article 368. 2. The Kesavananda Bharati case held that the Preamble can be amended, provided the amendment does not alter its basic structure. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Court held the Preamble can be amended under Article 368, but not so as to alter or destroy the basic structure or fundamental identity of the Constitution reflected in it.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the Berubari Union case (1960): 1. The Supreme Court held the Preamble to be a key to understanding the minds of the makers of the Constitution. 2. The Supreme Court held the Preamble to be enforceable in a court of law. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: In Berubari, the Court called the Preamble a key to the minds of the makers of the Constitution but held it was not part of the Constitution and hence not enforceable.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements comparing the original (1949) and current Preamble: 1. The current Preamble contains the words Socialist and Secular, which were absent in 1949. 2. The current Preamble refers to unity and integrity of the Nation, whereas the 1949 Preamble referred only to unity of the Nation. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both changes were introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, which added Socialist, Secular and changed unity to unity and integrity of the Nation.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Preamble was enacted as a separate legal instrument before the Constituent Assembly adopted the rest of the Constitution. 2. The Preamble uses the phrase IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY to refer to the body that adopted the Constitution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Preamble is part of the same Constitution adopted together, not a separate instrument; it does state IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the justiciability of the Preamble: 1. Since Kesavananda Bharati, the Preamble is part of the Constitution. 2. Being part of the Constitution automatically makes every term of the Preamble directly enforceable in a court like a Fundamental Right. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Although the Preamble is part of the Constitution, its terms are still considered non-justiciable; one cannot approach a court solely on the ground that the Preamble has been violated.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the words Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic and Republic in the Preamble: 1. All five words were part of the original 1949 Preamble. 2. Only Sovereign, Democratic and Republic were part of the original 1949 Preamble; Socialist and Secular were added later. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 1949 Preamble had only Sovereign Democratic Republic; Socialist and Secular were inserted later by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Berubari Union case was decided in 1960. 2. The Kesavananda Bharati case was decided in 1973. 3. The LIC of India case referred to here was decided in 1995. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three landmark cases relating to the status of the Preamble were decided in the years stated: 1960, 1973 and 1995 respectively.

advanced.q: In which case did the Supreme Court first hold that the Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution?
o: LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
advanced.e: In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution and hence not enforceable in court.

advanced.q: Which case overruled the Berubari view and held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
advanced.e: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court rejected its earlier Berubari stance and held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution.

advanced.q: The doctrine that emerged from the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), which also has a bearing on whether the Preamble itself can be amended, is known as the:
advanced.e: Kesavananda Bharati propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine, holding that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution, including the Preamble, so as to destroy its basic structure.

advanced.q: As per the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Preamble:
o: Can be freely amended without any restriction
Can be amended only by a Constituent Assembly, not Parliament
Can be amended under Article 368, but not so as to alter its basic structure
Can never be amended under any circumstances
advanced.e: The Court held the Preamble can be amended under Article 368, provided the amendment does not alter or destroy the basic structure or fundamental identity reflected in it.

advanced.q: Which case reiterated that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution, following the position taken in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995)
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
advanced.e: In the LIC of India case (1995), the Supreme Court reiterated that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution, following Kesavananda Bharati.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly captures the reasoning of the Supreme Court in the Berubari Union case regarding the utility of the Preamble?
o: The Preamble has no interpretative value and should be ignored by courts
The Preamble is a key to understanding the minds of the makers of the Constitution and useful where the language of an Article is ambiguous, though not enforceable itself
The Preamble is a part of the Constitution and fully justiciable
The Preamble is superior to all Fundamental Rights and directly enforceable
advanced.e: Berubari held the Preamble is a key to the minds of the makers useful for interpreting ambiguous Articles, but that it is not part of the Constitution and not enforceable in itself.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the evolution of judicial opinion on the Preamble is correct?
o: The Court has consistently held since 1960 that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution

The Court's position shifted from Berubari (1960), holding the Preamble was not part of the Constitution, to Kesavananda Bharati (1973), holding that it was, a stance later reaffirmed in LIC of India (1995)
The Court has never addressed whether the Preamble is part of the Constitution
The Court's position shifted from the Preamble being part of the Constitution (Berubari, 1960) to not being part of it (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973)
advanced.e: The judicial trajectory moved from Berubari (1960) - not part - to Kesavananda Bharati (1973) - part - and was reaffirmed in LIC of India (1995).

advanced.q: Despite being held to be a part of the Constitution since Kesavananda Bharati, why is the Preamble still considered distinct from provisions like Fundamental Rights?
o: It was never adopted by the Constituent Assembly
It applies only to Union Territories
Its terms are non-justiciable and cannot be directly enforced in a court of law on a standalone basis
It has been repealed by a subsequent constitutional amendment
advanced.e: Even as part of the Constitution, the Preamble remains non-justiciable - one cannot approach a court solely alleging violation of the Preamble, unlike Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Court's view that the Preamble is amendable but not so as to alter its basic structure implies which of the following?
o: Only the President can amend the Preamble by executive order
Values like Sovereign, Republic, or the unity/integrity of the Nation reflected in the Preamble cannot be removed or destroyed even by a constitutional amendment
Parliament can delete any word from the Preamble through an ordinary law
The Preamble is completely immune from amendment
advanced.e: The ruling means core values reflected in the Preamble, forming part of the Constitution's basic structure, are beyond the amending power of Parliament under Article 368, even though the wording of the Preamble itself can technically be changed.

advanced.q: Which of the following is a correct distinction between the Berubari Union case and the Kesavananda Bharati case with respect to the Preamble?
o: Both cases affirmed the Preamble's status as part of the Constitution using the same reasoning
Berubari affirmed the Preamble's status as part of the Constitution, while Kesavananda Bharati denied it
Berubari denied the Preamble's status as part of the Constitution, while Kesavananda Bharati affirmed it and also linked it to the basic structure doctrine
Both cases denied the Preamble's status as part of the Constitution
advanced.e: Berubari (1960) denied the Preamble was part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) affirmed it while also introducing the basic structure doctrine that constrains its amendment.

advanced.q: The only constitutional amendment made to the Preamble to date was upheld as constitutionally valid on the premise, established later in Kesavananda Bharati, that:
o: The Preamble was excluded from the scope of Article 368 in 1976
Only the Constituent Assembly, and not Parliament, could amend the Preamble
An amendment to the Preamble is valid so long as it does not destroy the basic structure of the Constitution
The Preamble cannot be amended at all, making the 42nd Amendment's changes void
advanced.e: Per Kesavananda Bharati, an amendment to the Preamble (such as the 42nd Amendment) is valid as long as it does not alter or destroy the basic structure or fundamental identity of the Constitution.

advanced.q: Which statement correctly reflects the Supreme Court's stance on whether the Preamble by itself is a source of substantive Fundamental Rights?
o: The Preamble was declared a Fundamental Right in Kesavananda Bharati
The Preamble is not itself a source of substantive rights enforceable independently in court, though it aids interpretation
The Preamble supersedes Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution
The Preamble is the primary and sole source of all Fundamental Rights
advanced.e: Courts have consistently held the Preamble is not an independent source of enforceable rights; it aids constitutional interpretation but does not confer justiciable rights on its own.

advanced.q: Consider the following with respect to landmark cases on the Preamble: 1. In re: The Berubari Union (1960) primarily dealt with a boundary/territorial dispute where the Preamble's status was discussed incidentally. 2. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) primarily dealt with the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
advanced.e: Berubari arose from a territorial matter (transfer of the Berubari Union), while Kesavananda Bharati centrally dealt with the scope of Parliament's amending power under Article 368, in which the basic structure doctrine and Preamble's status were addressed.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the LIC of India case (1995) is considered significant with regard to the Preamble, even though it did not overturn any prior precedent?
o: It held that the Preamble could no longer be amended after 1995
It reversed Kesavananda Bharati and restored the Berubari position
It reaffirmed and reinforced the settled position from Kesavananda Bharati that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
It was the first case to hold that the Preamble is enforceable exactly like Fundamental Rights
advanced.e: The LIC of India case is significant because it reiterated and reinforced settled law from Kesavananda Bharati that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution, rather than introducing a new rule.

advanced.q: A tricky distinction tested in exams is that being part of the Constitution (as held since Kesavananda Bharati) does NOT automatically mean the Preamble is:
o: Reflective of the Constitution's underlying philosophy and values
Amendable under Article 368 subject to the basic structure limitation
Directly enforceable/justiciable in a court of law
Available as an aid to interpreting ambiguous constitutional provisions
advanced.e: Even though the Preamble is part of the Constitution, it is not directly enforceable or justiciable; it remains useful for interpretation and is amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine, but courts cannot grant remedies solely for its violation.

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution declares "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"?
basic.e: Article 1 opens the Constitution with the declaration that India shall be a Union of States, and also defines the territory of India.

basic.q: As per Article 1, the territory of India comprises which of the following?
o: The territories of the States, the Union Territories specified in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired
Only the territories of the States
States and territories acquired by treaty only
basic.e: Article 1 defines India's territory broadly to include States, Union Territories in the First Schedule, and territories that may be acquired in future.

basic.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States?
basic.e: Article 2 allows Parliament to admit or establish new States on terms it thinks fit, covering territory not previously part of India.

basic.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to form a new State by separation of territory, unite states, increase or diminish area, alter boundaries, or alter the name of an existing State?
basic.e: Article 3 gives Parliament wide powers of internal reorganisation of existing Indian States' area, boundaries, and names.

basic.q: Which Article provides that a law made under Article 2 or Article 3 amending the First or Second Schedule shall not be deemed an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368?
basic.e: Article 4 exempts such laws from the Article 368 amendment procedure, allowing them to be passed as ordinary legislation.

basic.q: A bill under Article 3 to form a new State can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of whom?
basic.e: Article 3 bills require the prior recommendation of the President before introduction in Parliament.

basic.q: Under Article 3, if a bill affects the area, boundaries, or name of a State, to whom must the President refer the bill for its views?
basic.e: The President must refer such a bill to the concerned State Legislature for expressing its views within a specified period.

basic.q: On what date did the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 come into effect?
basic.e: The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 came into effect on 1 November 1956.

basic.q: In which year was the States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali Commission) appointed?
basic.e: The Fazl Ali Commission was appointed in 1953 to examine the reorganisation of state boundaries.

basic.q: Who chaired the States Reorganisation Commission?
basic.e: The Commission was chaired by Fazl Ali, with H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar as its other members.

basic.q: Besides Fazl Ali, who were the other two members of the States Reorganisation Commission?
basic.e: The other two members of the Commission were H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar.

basic.q: On what principal basis did the States Reorganisation Commission recommend the reorganisation of state boundaries?
basic.e: The Commission recommended reorganisation of states broadly on a linguistic basis.

basic.q: As a result of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, how many States and Union Territories were created?
basic.e: The Act created a structure of 14 States and 6 Union Territories, replacing the earlier classification.

basic.q: Which classification of states/territories, originally set out in the Constitution's First Schedule, was abolished by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956?
o: The Part A, Part B, Part C and Part D classification
basic.e: The earlier fourfold Part A, Part B, Part C, and Part D classification of states/territories was abolished by the 1956 Act.

basic.q: Which was the first State created purely on a linguistic basis, in 1953?
basic.e: Andhra State was carved out of the Madras Presidency in 1953, following the death of Potti Sriramulu, predating the SRC report and 1956 Act.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 1 of the Constitution:
1. It describes India as a "Union of States".
2. It states that the territory of India shall consist only of the territories of the States listed in the First Schedule.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
